choices:
Estimator: estimate = T + kappa*(F - R). T is design-weighted OLS (weights N_h/n_h) on audited rows with true values, R is the same regression with recorded values, and F is OLS on all rows with recorded values. This is a coefficient-level difference/GREG estimator, the same form for audited outcome and audited predictor. It keeps T's design consistency and uses the recorded values only as a control.

Tuning: kappa is a through-origin regression of T's cluster scores on R's, audited clusters only, clipped to [0, 2]. I chose this over minimizing the estimated variance across all clusters for two reasons. Algebra shows the optimum equals this slope regardless of audit fraction, and the audited-only form gives kappa = 1 and estimate = F exactly when recorded equals truth on all audited rows. The minimum-variance version was worse in testing: relative bias -0.21 and coverage 0.85 in the rare outcome cells.

Variance: sum over all clusters of (g_c + kappa*h_c)^2, with g_c = T score - kappa*R score and h_c = F score. There is no finite-population correction, because the target is the superpopulation coefficient, so the phase-one variance is kept through h_c. Scores use CR2 leverage adjustment, with a pseudo-inverse so a singleton stratum contributes only within-cluster information; I do not need to collapse strata. Three small-sample corrections apply:
(1) g_c is divided by (1 - lev), a leave-one-out correction for estimating kappa.
(2) lev is scaled by n_h/(n_h - 1), because stratum effects use up contrasts, and capped at 0.6.
(3) CR3 replaces CR2 when the response is a non-negative integer count, because count variance rises with leverage.

Degrees of freedom: Bell-McCaffrey Satterthwaite for the combined statistic, with the audited and all-row parts each scaled to their observed scores, capped by an empirical 3v^2/sum(s^4) that falls when one cluster dominates.

It calls stop() if the term is not estimable in the audited clusters, a stratum has no audited cluster, there are fewer than 3 audited rows, or the variance is zero. It uses base R only, has no randomness, and takes about 3 ms per call.

Tried and rejected, all on the predictor side unless noted:
- A surrogate from a working model of truth on recorded, covariate and outcome: width about 1 to 2% narrower or no better.
- Two tuned controls: no gain.
- An influence-function control with exact design mean zero: removed most of the bias, but widths were about 10 to 60% larger and it loses the exact-agreement property.
- Jackknife bias correction: removed bias in most cells, but coverage fell to as low as 0.85.
- Full CR3 throughout, on all cells: over-covered at about 0.97 and about 20 to 30% wider in the outcome cells than the final setup on the common error types.
own_simulations:
Compute was about 11 minutes wall time at 8 cores. Three tuning rounds used 400 reps per cell on 60 cells: 6 error types, rows = 3, fractions 0.25 and 0.5, designs rwanda/pairs/none for outcome and rwanda/pairs for predictor (the generator's predictor cell needs strata).

Final validation used fresh seeds, 500 reps per cell, Monte Carlo SE about 0.01 per cell. There were no failures. Mean coverage across cells was 0.950, minimum 0.894.

Coverage by error type, with mean relative width (interval width / target):
- Outcome: row_only 0.962 (0.60), shift_low 0.953 (0.73), shift 0.942 (0.74), under 0.942 (0.69), outlier 0.965 (0.74), rare 0.933 (3.01).
- Predictor: row_only 0.956 (0.42), shift_low 0.957 (0.46), shift 0.945 (0.44), under 0.956 (0.41), outlier 0.929 (0.51), rare 0.964 (3.47).

Weakest cells:
- Predictor outlier at fraction 0.25: 0.894 (pairs) and 0.908 (rwanda), with relative bias -0.053 averaged over the outlier cells.
- Outcome rare with no strata: 0.914 and 0.898.
- Outcome shift, pairs, 0.25: 0.920.

Comparators came from round 1 only (400 reps, same generator, different seeds, not rerun with the final corrections), so these comparisons are approximate.
- Audit-only T: relative width outcome shift 1.10, row_only 0.96, rare 4.42; predictor shift 0.54. The final setup is about 20 to 37% narrower on those four; the outcome rare comparison also has T coverage of only 0.90.
- Plain difference estimator (kappa = 1): outcome shift 0.85, under 0.67, row_only 0.63; predictor shift 0.44, under 0.47. The gain from tuning after the corrections is modest: about 13% on outcome shift, about 13% on predictor under, about 5% on outcome row_only, none on predictor shift, and about 3% wider on outcome under.

Extra scenarios used 300 reps per cell at fraction 0.25, 25 cells, no failures:
- Recorded exactly equal to truth: coverage 0.94 to 0.96, relative width about 0.39 to 0.42 outcome and 0.26 to 0.28 predictor.
- 3% sparse row errors or 5% sparse cluster errors: 0.94 to 0.98.
- Zero-heavy counts: 0.92 to 0.98, with predictor relative width about 8 and bias up to -0.17 in that cell.
- 210 clusters: 0.94.
- 6 rows per cluster: 0.957.
- 1 row per cluster: 0.947 to 0.963.
doubts:
- Weakest area: predictor with cluster-level outlier errors at fraction 0.25, coverage about 0.90. F - R has a small-sample ratio bias when few outlier clusters reach the audit, and the two fixes I tried cost too much (wider intervals or lost coverage), so it is left in and not corrected. Relative bias is also about -0.02 for predictor shift.
- Rare or heavy-tailed outcomes without strata remain near 0.90 even with CR3. Their skew is not fixable with a symmetric interval.
- Tuning risk: the leverage cap (0.6), the n_h/(n_h - 1) scaling and the count rule were all chosen on this generator. The final seeds were fresh but the generator was not, so the coverage figures are somewhat optimistic for real data.
- The count rule is a plain integer check. In the generator only the rare cells trigger it, so rounded continuous data would also get CR3 and wider intervals.
- It widens rare outcome intervals by about 20% compared with the CR2 version.
- Exact agreement: if every audited row agrees, the answer is F with its all-row variance and no allowance for errors in unaudited clusters. Rare large errors that the audit missed are not reflected in that interval. Coverage held in my sparse-error scenarios, but those errors were moderate (sd 10, about 5% of clusters).
- Singleton strata add only within-cluster information to T and R. If within-cluster and between-cluster slopes differ in real data, that gives mild design bias. The generator has the same slope in both, so I did not test this; I also did not test heterogeneous slopes across strata.
- Comparators were not rerun on the final seeds and the tuning gain is modest. A plain kappa = 1 difference estimator is a credible simpler choice.

choices:
mice is the driver (m = 30, maxit = 1, eps = 0, no collinearity removal). The statistics sit in my own elementary method, mice.impute.ind2l, not in a built-in, so mice is a thin wrapper here.

Imputation model. It targets the error d = gold - recorded, so exact agreement stays exact.
- Mundlak two-level model: separate within-cluster and between-cluster slopes on recorded, covariate and outcome (when allowed), plus a cluster random intercept.
- Why: stock 2l.lmer forces one slope across levels. Separate slopes keep second moments right at both levels even when the model is wrong, which is what a slope on an imputed predictor needs.
- Why not stock 2l.lmer: it also draws the random-intercept variance from shrunken BLUPs and refits an identical model m times.
- With one incomplete variable the posterior factors into a within regression and a between regression, so draws are exact for balanced clusters and need no chain. Unequal cluster sizes use a row-weighted approximation.
- sigma_b^2 is drawn truncated below at sigma^2/k.

Strata. They get empirical-Bayes partial pooling in the between regression. Fixed strata left about 7 to 8 between df on 17 clusters, which widened intervals and worsened attenuation. Dropping and pooling performed alike in the generator; I kept pooling as protection against stratum-level errors.

Imputed predictor only: residual variances are deflated, by a factor of about (df-2)/df - 2p/G, floored at 0.1. Proper draws inflate the variance of the imputed value and attenuate the slope. This is a deliberate, heuristic departure from proper MI.

Analysis. OLS on completed data with CR3 cluster variance and Bell-McCaffrey df. I chose CR3 over CR2 because even with all rows audited, CR2 covered rare counts at only 0.88 to 0.89.

Pooling. Rubin's total variance. The reference df is Satterthwaite, combining the analysis df with the between-regression df on audited clusters plus 1/(m-1). The Barnard-Rubin df collapsed to about 3 to 5 and produced huge intervals.

Other cases.
- All audited rows agree exactly: return the analysis of recorded values with B = 0.
- Refuses only when fewer than 3 between df remain (or on a rank-deficient model, or if the audit does not cover whole clusters).
- fit_method assigns the method into globalenv, because mice only finds elementary methods there.
own_simulations:
Compute was about 13 minutes wall time and roughly 2,100 CPU-seconds, at most 8 cores.

Final setup: 60 cells (6 error types, fractions 0.25 and 0.5, rwanda/pairs/none for outcome, rwanda/pairs for predictor), 100 reps each, no refusals. MCSE of coverage per cell is about 2 points, so single-cell values are noisy.

Mean coverage across cells:
| Case | Fraction 0.25 | Fraction 0.5 |
|---|---|---|
| Audited outcome | 0.965 | 0.961 |
| Audited predictor | 0.953 | 0.967 |

Outcome, by error type (excluding rare, which is below):
- Coverage 0.96 to 0.98, relative bias within about 1.6%, SE/SD 1.03 to 1.18.
- Relative half-width about 0.35 to 0.47 at 0.25 and 0.26 to 0.35 at 0.5.

Predictor, by error type:
- Coverage 0.945 to 0.975, mean relative bias within 2% except outlier (-3.8%).
- Relative half-width about 0.21 to 0.27 at 0.25 and 0.16 to 0.21 at 0.5 (rare excluded).

Rare counts: outcome coverage 0.89 to 0.93, predictor 0.96 to 0.98, relative half-width about 1.4 to 1.9.

Weakest cells:
- Predictor, pairs, outlier, 0.25: coverage 0.90, SE/SD 0.78, bias -4.9%.
- Predictor, rwanda, outlier, 0.25: bias -7.1%, coverage 0.96.
- Predictor, rwanda, under, 0.25: coverage 0.91.
- Outcome, none, rare, 0.5: coverage 0.89.

Run time was about 0.07 s per call for outcome and 0.2 s for predictor. The first call in a session takes 2 to 3 s to load the namespace.

What each choice changed (rwanda design, 100 to 250 reps per cell, on earlier versions with m = 20, CR2 at the time):
- Stock 2l.lmer with a wrapper, same analysis (50 reps): predictor, shift, 0.25 had bias -12.8% and coverage 0.82. Final setup in the same cell: +1.6% and 0.95. In the other three cells tested the stock version was not clearly worse on bias (outcome +2.0% and -2.6%, predictor row_only +2.7%), but its df was lower and its outcome half-widths wider (0.50 vs 0.46).
- Barnard-Rubin to Satterthwaite df: median df about 3 to 5 became about 17 to 25; outcome half-width at 0.25 fell from about 0.86 to 0.36 with coverage 0.98 in both (row_only, strata dropped).
- Deflation at 0.25, predictor: bias went from -7.0% to -1.4% (row_only) and -4.7% to -0.5% (under). Outlier bias went from -9.6% to -5.4%, but its coverage fell from 0.935 to 0.885.
- CR2 to CR3, rare: rwanda outcome at 0.5 rose from 0.85 to 0.92. All-rows-audited coverage rose from 0.88/0.89 to 0.91/0.92, while shift rose from 0.95/0.94 to 0.97/0.96.

My own scenarios outside the generator (rwanda-shaped cohorts, outcome, fraction 0.25, 160 reps; slightly different seeds from a plain re-run are irrelevant to these figures):
| Scenario | Coverage | SE/SD | Relative half-width |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exact agreement on all rows | 0.963 | 1.05 | 0.284 |
| 5% of rows disagree | 0.975 | 1.09 | 0.299 |
| Correlation above 0.99 | 0.950 | 1.05 | 0.288 |
| Stratum-specific errors | 0.969 | 1.13 | 0.427 |
| About 30% of rows dropped (unbalanced) | 0.981 | 1.15 | 0.402 |
| Zero-heavy counts (155 of 160 usable) | 0.948 | 0.97 | 1.597 |

The 5 unusable zero-heavy cohorts came from a bug in my scenario: negative Poisson rates gave NA truth (5 NA warnings). I confirmed the error message on the two I could see. They are not a defect found in the method, but those cohorts do refuse, correctly, when audited truth is NA.

I did not run an audit-only comparator in the final grid, so I have no measured precision gain to report.
doubts:
Weakest area: heavy-tailed cluster errors with few audited clusters, especially the audited predictor with outliers at 0.25. The model is linear-Gaussian. If no outlier cluster falls in the audit (about 17% of 17-cluster audits at a 10% outlier rate), the imputed values keep those errors and the interval cannot know. If one is audited, it dominates the between regression. Deflation made this case worse on coverage (0.935 to 0.885 in the comparison run, 0.90 to 0.96 in the final grid) while cutting bias there and elsewhere, so it is a real trade-off.

Rare counts on the audited outcome still fall a little short (0.89 to 0.93). The cause looks like the full-cohort analysis under heavy tails, not the imputation, since coverage is only 0.91 to 0.92 with all rows audited. Real counts could behave worse than this generator.

The deflation factor and the Satterthwaite df are my own heuristics, justified by moment arguments and tuned on this generator. They are not published MI theory. Tuning and final checks used the same generator with different seeds, so these numbers are not independent validation, and they may flatter the setup.

The setup is conservative on many non-rare outcome cells (coverage up to 1.00, SE/SD up to 1.32), partly from CR3, so intervals there are wider than necessary.

When every audited row agrees exactly, B = 0 and the interval reflects no recording error at all. Errors in unaudited clusters would be invisible. I chose not to add an ad hoc inflation.

Unbalanced clusters use an approximation (harmonic-mean k, row-weighted between regression). I tested it in only one scenario, audited outcome only. Errors that depend strongly on x in variance are not modeled, and the predictor case outside the generator was not stress-tested. Exact-agreement and near-agreement scenarios were also outcome only.

The 100 reps per cell cannot separate cells 2 points apart. The stock comparison used only 50 reps in 4 cells.

The empirical-Bayes strata step has a floor case: when every stratum has one audited cluster it is skipped, so a real stratum effect is absorbed in the between residual. A small design-weight mismatch from unequal stratum fractions is ignored, since the imputation does not weight.

choices:
Method: a two-phase regression (GREG) estimator using survey::calibrate (linear, weights constant within cluster, starting from design weights N_h/n_h).

1. Nuisance terms are partialled out on phase 1, not refit in the audited sample. I started with the textbook setup: influence-function auxiliaries with a weighted fit including stratum effects on audited rows. It did poorly. With 1 or 2 audited clusters per stratum, stratum effects are re-estimated from almost nothing, and the phase-1 influence function barely correlates with the audited fit. So I partial out strata (plus the covariate in the predictor case) on all rows and estimate the unknown normal-equation totals with calibrated weights.
- Audited outcome: beta = sum(xt*truth)/sum(xt^2), with auxiliaries xt*lab, xt^2, xt.
- Audited predictor: beta = sum(ts*yt)/sum(ts^2), with auxiliaries ths*yt, ths^2, where ths is an imputation from lab, covariate, outcome and an empirical-Bayes stratum offset. The eps pitfall does not arise because this uses lm.wfit, not mice.
- When all audited rows agree exactly, the estimate is the phase-1 fit.

2. Predictor-only guards.
- The stratum offset removes a denominator bias that I found under stratum-specific error offsets.
- Cluster-mean imputed values are clamped to the audited range, so unseen outlier clusters do not extrapolate through the squared auxiliary. This is switched off for count-like values and for exact agreement.

3. Variance is V1 + V2, with no fpc, because the phase-2 fpc cancels against the residual part of phase 1 for a superpopulation target.
- V1 is a leverage-corrected delete-cluster variance of the auxiliary part over all clusters. This avoids the zero phase-1 variance of twophase(method="full"), because I do not use twophase.
- For non-negative integer recorded values with an audited outcome, V1 is floored by a smooth mean-variance working model (c1 m^2 + c2 m).
- V2 is a delete-one-audited-cluster jackknife with re-imputation and re-calibration, with all audited clusters in one collapsed group. This handles leverage, and singleton strata need no special rule.

4. df is Satterthwaite of G-H-1 and n-1.

5. Rejected after testing:
- Leverage-based effective df (over-conservative on top of the jackknife).
- A cluster bootstrap-t df (coverage about +2 points for about +30% width in rare cells).
- Dropping the squared auxiliary (bad in rare and exact cells).
- A row-level clamp (weaker than the cluster-level clamp).

survey::calibrate gives the point-estimate weights. Replicates use the equivalent closed form for speed; weights matched to the 6 decimals printed on the 10 outcome fixtures, and the survey branch did not fall back on the one fixture I traced. It uses no randomness, so seed is unused.
own_simulations:
Final run: 120 cells at 300 reps each (36,000 fits), rows = 3. Cells cover designs rwanda, pairs and none for outcome and rwanda, pairs for predictor, fractions 0.25 and 0.5, the 6 generator error types, and 6 stress variants I added: exact agreement, 2% errors, stratum offset, stratum multiplier, rare exact, rare 2% slip. Refusals 0. Mean 0.017 s per call, max 0.36 s, on a loaded machine. Monte Carlo SE of each coverage is about 1.3 points.

Coverage, mean across cells (min to max):
- Generator non-rare errors: outcome 0.955 (0.927 to 0.980), predictor 0.964 (0.933 to 0.987).
- Rare-type, which pools generator rare with my rare exact and rare 2% slip cells: outcome 0.937 (0.893 to 0.967), predictor 0.948 (0.920 to 0.973).
- Other stress cells: outcome 0.944 (0.910 to 0.967), predictor 0.949 (0.920 to 0.973).

Typical rwanda outcome cells at 0.25: mean of SD 0.12, mean width 0.59. Same at 0.5: SD 0.089, width 0.38. Rwanda predictor at 0.25: SD 0.059, width 0.27. At 0.5: SD 0.044, width 0.20. Bias is about 0.02 or less in magnitude in the non-rare cells; it stays small relative to SD in rare predictor cells, whose SD is about 0.3 to 0.4.

Comparisons from earlier rounds (200 reps):
- Textbook weighted fit with stratum effects, pairs at 0.25, 6 generator errors: SD 0.143, against 0.093 for the phase-1 partialled form. With collapsed jackknife, coverage 0.98 at width 0.96, against 0.94 at width 0.43. With stratified jackknife, coverage fell to 0.73.
- Count floor: outcome rare-type coverage rose from about 0.82-0.90 to about 0.89-0.95 at about 15-25% more width. Even with exact agreement and no floor it was about 0.85, a phase-1 inference problem with heavy tails (empirical 2.5% and 97.5% t quantiles about -3.5 and +1.6).
- Predictor outlier at 0.25, before and after clamp plus offset: bias -0.03 to about -0.005, SD 0.07 to 0.06, coverage 0.92 to 0.95. Predictor stratum offset at 0.5 (my stress cell): coverage 0.81 to 0.95.

I did not run survey::twophase itself as a comparator. Wall-clock simulation time was about 11 minutes, within the 15-minute limit, at 8 cores.
doubts:
- Tuning risk: the count floor, cluster clamp and stratum offset were chosen by looking at this generator and my own stress cells, with no held-out generator. The floor's mean-variance form suits the gamma frailty here and may not fit real zero-heavy counts.
- Weakest area: audited-outcome rare counts in stratified designs. Rwanda rare-type averaged 0.92-0.93, with single cells down to 0.89 (pairs rare exact at 0.5). The error is skewed and a symmetric interval cannot fix that. The floor triggers only on non-negative integer values, so skewed continuous values get no protection.
- Exact agreement: V2 is exactly 0, so the SE is phase-1 only. An audit that sees no errors cannot rule out errors in unaudited clusters, and such errors at unknown size would not be covered.
- Conservatism: the collapsed jackknife runs wide at fraction 0.25. In the first round, SE/SD was often 1.2-1.4 in non-rare cells. That width costs power, and I accepted it to get singleton-stratum handling and leverage protection.
- Linear calibration has no bounds, so calibrated weights can go negative. On the rare fixture the range was -10 to 35. I left this because results looked fine, but it signals strong extrapolation on sparse auxiliaries.
- The clamp makes the jackknife non-smooth when an audited outlier cluster sets the limit. A count-like column with large integers and true outliers gets no clamp.
- Small bias remains in the predictor denominator: about +0.02 under stratum offsets at 0.25.
- With 300 reps per cell, individual minimums are partly noise, and I did not run a higher-rep confirmation.
- The survey package supplies only the point-estimate calibration. All variance code is hand-written, so survey's own variance machinery does not check it.
